title: ToolOPD: Credit-Aware On-Policy Distillation for Tool-Use Agents

paper.title: ToolOPD: Credit-Aware On-Policy Distillation for Tool-Use Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) enhances the capabilities of small language agents by providing dense, token-level supervision from a teacher model on student-generated trajectories. However, standard OPD implicitly assumes that credit is uniformly distributed across long-horizon trajectories, assigning the same strength of teacher supervision to different actions. Through credit-distribution analysis and outcome-reversal counterfactual experiments, we find that trajectory credit is concentrated on a small number of critical actions. Moreover, even when the trajectory is held fixed, reversing only the final outcome substantially changes the credit assigned to multiple interaction turns. These findings show that the uniform-credit assumption fails to identify critical decisions and ultimately degrades the model’s reasoning accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose ToolOPD , an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework designed for long-horizon tool use. ToolOPD first summarizes each completed trajectory and
its outcome into a reusable hindsight skill. It then measures how this skill changes the teacher’s probability of each student action token and converts the change into outcome-aware credit. The resulting credit preserves supervision that supports successful decisions or discourages failed ones, while suppressing irrelevant and conflicting signals. ToolOPD uses these credits to reweight the action-level distillation loss and jointly optimizes it with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across multiple long-horizon tool interaction benchmarks demonstrate that ToolOPD significantly outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Empirical Study Results. Large language models (LLMs) ( Naveed et al., 2025 ; Minaee et al., 2024 ; Chang et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2026b ; Thirunavukarasu et al., 2023 ) have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex interactive tasks by invoking external tools ( Qu et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Qin et al., 2024 ) and adapting their decisions to environmental feedback. However, long-horizon tool-use tasks ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) often require tens or hundreds of interaction turns while providing only a sparse success-or-failure reward at the end of the trajectory. This makes it difficult to determine which intermediate actions contribute to the final outcome. On-policy distillation (OPD) ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Song and Zheng, 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) addresses sparse supervision by matching a compact student policy to a teacher distribution on trajectories generated by the student itself. Standard OPD implicitly assumes that credit is uniformly distributed across long-horizon trajectories, such that different actions receive equal credit and the same strength of teacher supervision. This uniform credit assignment fails to distinguish critical tool decisions from routine transitional actions, thereby weakening effective supervision for critical decisions. To systematically characterize this issue, we conduct a series of empirical studies. As shown in Fig. 1 (a), on the ALFWorld diagnostic trajectories, the top 20% of interaction turns account for 74.2% of the total credit, demonstrating that trajectory credit is highly concentrated rather than uniformly distributed. We further construct an outcome-reversal counterfactual experiment by fixing the complete task and state–action sequence while reversing only the outcome label provided to the teacher. Fig. 1 (b) shows that this intervention substantially changes the credit assigned to 55.2%, 25.0%, and 50.0% of interaction turns in ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA, respectively. Thus, the credit of an action depends not only on its local context but also on its relationship with the final outcome. Fig. 1 (c) further shows that outcome-conflicting signals account for 53.5% of the total teacher evidence under uniform distillation. Together, these findings establish that effective long-horizon distillation must identify critical actions and determine whether the corresponding teacher signals are consistent with the trajectory outcome. Detailed settings are provided in Appendix H . Recent studies have begun to explore fine-grained credit assignment for long-horizon tasks. ATOD ( Tan et al., 2026b ) adaptively adjusts the distillation strength of different actions according to the discrepancy between the teacher and student policies, while TurnSight ( Qu et al., 2026b ) constructs multi-view hindsight information from actual tool executions and selects reliable turn-level supervision through cross-view consistency. Unlike existing methods that determine distillation weights from local teacher–student divergence, training progress, or interaction difficulty, in this work, we propose ToolOPD , an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework for long-horizon tool use. ToolOPD uses the terminal outcome to determine both the direction and strength of action credit. For each student-generated trajectory, ToolOPD conditions the teacher on the complete interaction process and its outcome to induce a concise hindsight skill that summarizes the effective workflow or failure pattern. It then compares the teacher’s action probabilities with and without the hindsight skill to estimate the outcome-relevant credit of each action token. For successful trajectories, ToolOPD retains skill-induced probability increases that reinforce effective actions; for failed trajectories, it retains probability decreases that suppress erroneous actions. The resulting relevance is further calibrated by teacher confidence and experience-based reliability to prevent uncertain or historically inconsistent teacher signals from dominating the update. ToolOPD uses the calibrated credit to dynamically reweight the distillation loss over <action> tokens and jointly optimizes it with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . This design concentrates supervision on outcome-relevant decisions while filtering redundant and conflicting signals. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • Empirical findings. We show that credit in long-horizon OPD is concentrated on critical actions and depends on trajectory outcomes, while uniform distillation transfers outcome-conflicting supervision. • Method. We propose ToolOPD, which induces outcome-conditioned hindsight skills and converts their effects on teacher predictions into fine-grained, outcome-asymmetric action credit. • Experiments. Across multiple tool-use benchmarks and model scales, ToolOPD consistently outperforms representative reinforcement learning and OPD baselines in task performance, long-context robustness, and optimization stability.

sections.heading: 2.1 Problem Formulation
sections.text: We consider multi-turn tool use tasks with a discrete set of executable actions. For a given task instance x i x_{i} , the student policy π θ \pi_{\theta} interacts with the external environment and generates a trajectory: τ i = { ( s i , t , a i , t , o i , t + 1 ) } t = 0 T i − 1 , \tau_{i}=\left\{(s_{i,t},a_{i,t},o_{i,t+1})\right\}_{t=0}^{T_{i}-1}, (1) where s i , t s_{i,t} denotes the interaction history and the current environmental state at step t t , a i , t ∈ 𝒜 ⁡ ( s i , t ) a_{i,t}\in\mathcal{A}(s_{i,t}) is the action selected by the student policy, and o i , t + 1 o_{i,t+1} is the observation feedback returned by the environment. Upon the termination of the trajectory, the environment returns a scalar task reward R i R_{i} and a binary outcome indicator y i = 𝕀 ⁡ ( R i > 0 ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{i}=\mathbb{I}(R_{i}>0)\in\{0,1\} . In long-horizon tool use scenarios, this setting introduces severe credit assignment challenges: due to the extremely long interaction horizon and highly sparse rewards, the success or failure of a task is typically determined by only a few critical tool decisions (e.g., specific API selections or parameter settings), while the vast majority of the remaining turns consist of routine state queries and transitional actions. How to accurately attribute and assign the terminal global reward to the intermediate specific actions is the core difficulty in optimizing such policies. We are given a teacher model π ϕ \pi_{\phi} with frozen parameters. Our objective is to distill the transferable strategy summarized by the teacher based on the complete trajectory and the final outcome into the student, while preserving the exploration capability of on-policy reinforcement learning. The trajectories during training are generated entirely by the current student policy, i.e., τ i ∼ π θ \tau_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta} . Therefore, our method falls under the category of On-Policy Distillation, rather than simple behavior cloning on offline teacher trajectories.

sections.heading: 2.2 Overview of ToolOPD
sections.text: To address the credit assignment dilemma caused by sparse rewards in long-horizon interactions, ToolOPD organically integrates GRPO with outcome-aware on-policy distillation. Its core idea is to transform sparse trajectory-level credit into dense action-level credit. The specific data flow is as follows: First, the student policy interacts with the environment to generate a set of on-policy trajectories, and the intra-group relative advantages for GRPO are computed. Subsequently, the teacher reads the complete trajectory and the final success/failure outcome to induce a concise, reusable hindsight skill. Next, by comparing the probability distributions of the teacher with and without this skill on the student’s actions, the outcome relevance of the skill to the current action is calculated, thereby achieving fine-grained credit assignment. Finally, a weighted teacher-to-student OPD is performed exclusively on the action ( <action> ) tokens. Throughout the training process, the teacher model parameters remain frozen, and all gradients are used solely to update the student model. The framework of ToolOPD is illustrated in Fig. 2 . Figure 2: ToolOPD framework overview.

sections.heading: 2.3 Outcome-Conditioned Hindsight Skill Induction
sections.text: Standard distillation typically directly imitates the local action distribution of the teacher, but the teacher lacks global perception of the final success or failure of the current trajectory in this process. To address this issue, ToolOPD first introduces a hindsight skill induction mechanism, allowing the teacher to distill experience using the complete trajectory and the final outcome: z i = G ϕ ​ ( τ i , y i ) , z_{i}=G_{\phi}(\tau_{i},y_{i}), (2) where G ϕ G_{\phi} denotes the skill induction process of the teacher. For successful trajectories ( y i = 1 y_{i}=1 ), the teacher summarizes effective operational procedures or key decisions; for failed trajectories ( y i = 0 y_{i}=0 ), the teacher identifies the root cause of the error and provides a general rule to avoid it. To facilitate context injection, the skill is constrained to a single concise rule, formatted as: Rule Name: imperative guidance. This design serves a dual purpose: first, it compresses lengthy interaction trajectories into reusable strategy priors, essentially distilling the macroscopic outcome credit at the trajectory level into microscopic strategy signals that can guide specific decisions; second, it prevents the teacher from directly rewriting the complete trajectory, thereby focusing the distillation signal on high-level decision-making patterns. All states within the same trajectory share the corresponding skill z i z_{i} for that trajectory. During the inference phase, the student can be deployed independently without the teacher or explicit skill generation, thus incurring no additional inference cost.

sections.heading: 3.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Benchmarks . We evaluate our method on two major categories of benchmarks to comprehensively assess the model’s performance across tool-use scenarios of varying complexity. The first category consists of classic agent interaction benchmarks, including the text-embodied environment ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2020 ) , SearchQA ( Jin et al., 2025 ) covering single-hop and multi-hop question answering, and the interactive online shopping environment WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) . The second category comprises benchmarks specifically designed for complex tool invocation, including the FTRL Ye et al. (2026) dataset, which covers single-step, sequential, and parallel tool-calling scenarios, and the BFCL ( Patil et al., 2025 ) and ToolHop ( Ye et al., 2025 ) dataset, which focus on evaluating long-horizon reasoning and execution capabilities with multi-step tool dependencies. Detailed descriptions are provided in the Appendix A . Baselines. We compare ToolOPD against three categories of methods: (1) Training-free : Vanilla (the instruction-tuned model without task-specific training). (2) Outcome RL and General (Self-) Distillation : including GRPO ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , ToolRL ( Qian et al., 2026 ) , and MatchTIR ( Qu et al., 2026a ) which optimize outcome rewards, as well as OPD, TCOD ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) , ATOD ( Tan et al., 2026b ) , and TurnSight ( Qu et al., 2026b ) which employ general distillation without explicit skill construction. (3) Skill-Conditioned Self-Distillation : Skill-SD ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , SDAR ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , and AgentOPSD ( Wang et al., 2026c ) , which incorporate skill guidance or trajectory reflection mechanisms. Details of each baseline are provided in the Appendix B . Training Details . All experiments are conducted on 8 A800 GPUs. We adopt Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B as student models, and a Qwen3-4B model trained with GRPO (150-step checkpoint) as the teacher model. In Table 1 , the training and optimization setups for ALFWorld, SearchQA, and WebShop are kept consistent with the AgentOPSD baseline. In Table 2, the models are trained exclusively on the FTRL dataset, with the remaining datasets used for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization evaluation, and their base parameter settings aligned with TurnSight. sections.heading: 3.2 Main Results
sections.text: Tables 1 and 2 present the performance of ToolOPD across various tool-use benchmarks. Overall, ToolOPD significantly outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines in all evaluated scenarios, validating its effectiveness in addressing the credit assignment problem in long-horizon tool use. Credit Assignment Breakthrough in Long-Horizon Interactions (Table 1 ). In long-horizon interaction tasks such as ALFWorld, SearchQA, and WebShop, task success or failure is typically determined by only a few critical tool decisions. Compared to pure reinforcement learning methods (e.g., GRPO), ToolOPD achieves substantial improvements (e.g., the success rate of Qwen3-0.6B on WebShop jumps from 10.9% to 58.6%), demonstrating that dense and precise token-level supervision can effectively overcome the credit assignment failure caused by terminal sparse rewards. Furthermore, compared to standard OPD, which implicitly assumes uniform weights (tending to distribute gradients across redundant actions), and AgentOPSD, which lacks outcome filtering, ToolOPD precisely quantifies and amplifies the weights of critical actions that substantially contribute to the final outcome through the outcome-asymmetric mechanism ( H i , t H_{i,t} ), fundamentally overcoming the dilution of core decision signals. Complex Tool Dependencies and Generalization Capabilities (Table 2 ). Across the FTRL, BFCL, and ToolHop benchmarks, ToolOPD not only achieves the highest average performance on the FTRL training set but also demonstrates strong generalization capabilities on out-of-distribution (OOD) test sets such as ToolHop and BFCL. Particularly in the ToolHop task, which features extremely long interaction turns and a large number of ineffective retrievals, ToolOPD significantly outperforms the second-best baseline, SDAR (improving the accuracy of Qwen3-1.7B from 19.0% to 22.2%). This is attributed to ToolOPD’s hindsight skill induction mechanism, which compresses macroscopic trajectory outcomes into microscopic strategy priors, combined with asymmetric relevance to truncate gradients for ineffective actions. This ensures that the model can precisely pinpoint core API calls within long-horizon trajectories, effectively enhancing reasoning and execution capabilities under complex state transitions. sections.heading: 3.3 Ablation Study
sections.text: To investigate the contribution of each component in ToolOPD to long-horizon credit assignment, we conduct a progressive ablation study on the ALFWorld benchmark, as reported in Table 3 . GRPO, which relies solely on sparse trajectory-level rewards, achieves an average success rate of only 14.8%, highlighting the limitation of sequence-level supervision in identifying pivotal decisions during long-horizon tool interactions. Incorporating standard action-level distillation substantially improves the average success rate to 53.9%, demonstrating that dense teacher supervision over action tokens provides effective local learning signals. However, Vanilla OPD assigns relatively uniform distillation weights across interaction steps and therefore cannot adequately distinguish pivotal decisions from redundant actions. Further introducing hindsight skill conditioning yields only a marginal improvement to 54.7%, with performance degradation on several task categories. This result suggests that skill conditioning alone does not guarantee consistent gains, as the model must additionally determine whether the induced skill is aligned with the trajectory outcome and whether the corresponding teacher signal is reliable. The complete ToolOPD combines outcome-asymmetric skill relevance H i , t H_{i,t} with teacher confidence and experience-based reliability to emphasize actions that are more relevant to the final outcome. It achieves the best average success rate of 59.4%, outperforming Vanilla OPD and Skill-OPD by 5.5 and 4.7 percentage points, respectively. The largest gains over Skill-OPD occur on Look, Clean, and Heat, with improvements of 25.0, 20.5, and 14.3 points. These results show that outcome-aware relevance and reliability calibration are critical for robust credit assignment in long-horizon tool interactions. (a) Teacher-student gap. sections.heading: 3.4 Training Dynamics
sections.text: Figure 3 presents the training dynamics of different methods across multiple tool-interaction benchmarks. ToolOPD achieves faster and more sustained performance improvements on ALFWorld and WebShop, establishing a clear advantage over the baselines in the later stages of training. Although the differences among methods are smaller on SearchQA, ToolOPD still attains the best final performance. These results suggest that its benefits are not specific to a particular environment, but generalize across tasks with different interaction horizons and reward structures. Meanwhile, the teacher–student gap in Figure 3(a) is not monotonically minimized toward zero, but instead changes dynamically throughout training. This behavior indicates that ToolOPD does not uniformly imitate all teacher signals; rather, it adaptively adjusts the strength of distillation according to the current policy state and trajectory outcome. Fig. 4 further characterizes the optimization behavior underlying these performance gains. On FTRL, ToolOPD maintains a consistently small and stable teacher–student discrepancy, whereas the discrepancies of MatchTIR and TurnSight progressively increase during training. Correspondingly, ToolOPD improves its F1 score more rapidly and reaches a higher level in the middle and later stages. On ALFWorld, the policy entropy of ToolOPD decreases substantially while its success rate continues to improve, suggesting that the policy gradually shifts from broad exploration toward more concentrated tool decisions rather than merely suffering from performance degradation. The entropy dynamics on FTRL exhibit a similar pattern: ToolOPD shows a smoother increase in entropy and avoids the pronounced growth in uncertainty observed for TurnSight. Overall, these results indicate that outcome-aware dynamic distillation enables ToolOPD to control teacher–student discrepancy while progressively focusing optimization on critical actions, leading to a more stable and efficient policy learning process. sections.heading: 3.6 Further Analysis of Credit Assignment
sections.text: To further examine the credit assignment capability of ToolOPD, we analyze both performance gains and supervision quality. As shown in Fig. 6 (a), ToolOPD achieves an average success rate of 59.38%, outperforming Vanilla OPD and Skill-OPD by 5.47 and 4.69 percentage points, respectively. This result indicates that dense distillation or hindsight skills alone are insufficient to achieve optimal performance. Fig. 6 (b) further explains the source of this improvement. When considering only the top 10%–20% highest-credit turns, the proportion of outcome-aligned signals reaches approximately 71.3%, substantially higher than random turns (approximately 50.0%) and bottom-credit turns (approximately 37.6%). As the retained proportion increases, the differences gradually diminish and eventually converge. These results demonstrate that ToolOPD effectively ranks turns according to supervision quality and prioritizes distillation signals associated with tool decisions that are more likely to affect the final outcome. Taken together, Fig. 6 (a) and (b) suggest that the performance gains of ToolOPD primarily arise from fine-grained, outcome-aware credit assignment, rather than merely introducing additional teacher supervision.

sections.heading: 4.1 On-policy Distillation
sections.text: On-policy distillation (OPD) ( Song and Zheng, 2026 ) aligns the student and teacher policies by matching the student policy to the teacher distribution over its self-generated trajectories. By utilizing objectives such as token-level KL divergence, OPD effectively mitigates the state distribution shift inherent in offline distillation. As OPD is extended to long-horizon agent tasks, research has transitioned from uniform token-level matching to step- or turn-level supervision. In Toolintegrated scenarios, existing approaches primarily operate along two dimensions. First, they leverage dynamic skills or hindsight information from completed trajectories to guide self-distillation (including Skill-SD ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , SEED ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , and TurnSight Qu et al. (2026b) ). Second, they dynamically adjust the distillation weights across interaction turns based on factors including teacher-student divergence, training budgets, and interaction difficulty (including SOD ( Zhong et al., 2026 ) , TurnOPD ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , AgentOPSD ( Wang et al., 2026c ) , and HIDIFFTIR ( Guo et al., 2026 ) ). These studies demonstrate that online distillation for Toolusing agents must model multi-turn interaction structures, tool invocation difficulty, and hindsight information, rather than relying on uniform token-level supervision. In contrast to existing methods, this paper focuses on the credit assignment problem for small models executing tool invocations in long-horizon tasks on resource-constrained terminal devices. We propose ToolOPD, which moves beyond the reliance on local training difficulty or teacher-student divergence by directly evaluating the true contribution of tool decisions based on final task outcomes. The core of ToolOPD lies in performing non-uniform credit assignment for distinct tool decisions and dynamically adjusting the distillation intensity of action tokens accordingly, thereby maximizing the distillation efficacy of small models under resource constraints.

sections.heading: 4.2 Credit Assignment in Long-Horizon On-Policy Distillation
sections.text: In long-horizon tool use tasks ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2026 ) , standard OPD typically performs uniform token-level distribution matching across all visited states. However, because different interaction turns contribute unequally to task success, applying supervision with uniform intensity is highly prone to introducing noise. Recent studies have introduced fine-grained credit assignment into long-horizon interactions and policy distillation. Some methods evaluate intermediate action values by quantifying information gain, leveraging hindsight information, or decomposing trajectory-level outcomes (e.g., Δ \Delta Belief-RL ( Auzina et al., 2026 ) , HCAPO ( Tan et al., 2026a ) , and PBSD ( Tian et al., 2026 ) ). Others identify critical action spans and adjust local advantages from the perspectives of supervision reliability, failure correlation, or policy comparison (e.g., Prune-OPD ( Yang et al., 2026b ) , HINT-SD ( Yeo et al., 2026 ) , UCOB ( Tu et al., 2026 ) , and SGCD ( Ding et al., 2026 ) ). Overall, existing research has transitioned from uniform token-level matching to credit-aware selective supervision. In this work, ToolOPD locates critical tool decisions by quantifying the shift in the teacher’s action distribution conditioned on hindsight skills. It then performs multi-dimensional credit calibration by integrating the final outcome, trajectory consistency, and teacher confidence. Ultimately, the calibrated turn-level credit is directly mapped to the action tokens actually sampled by the student, achieving non-uniform on-policy distillation oriented towards long-horizon task outcomes.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduce ToolOPD, an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework that addresses credit assignment in long-horizon tool-use tasks. Our empirical analysis shows that the uniform supervision of standard OPD fails to distinguish the contributions of different tool decisions and may introduce teacher signals that conflict with the final outcome. To address this limitation, ToolOPD induces hindsight skills from complete trajectories and their outcomes, and dynamically assigns credit to action tokens through outcome-asymmetric skill relevance. This preserves supervision consistent with the task outcome while suppressing irrelevant or conflicting signals. Experiments across multiple long-horizon tool-interaction benchmarks and model scales demonstrate that ToolOPD consistently outperforms reinforcement-learning and on-policy-distillation baselines while exhibiting more stable optimization over extended interactions.

sections.text: Contents

sections.heading: Appendix A Benchmarks
sections.text: • ALFWorld is an interactive benchmark that aligns abstract textual reasoning with concrete embodied environments, requiring agents to translate high-level text policies into multi-step navigation and object manipulation actions in simulated household settings, thereby evaluating cross-modal grounding and long-horizon planning. • SearchQA is a large-scale open-domain question answering dataset comprising over 140,000 question-answer pairs augmented with real-world search engine contexts, designed to assess model robustness in precise machine reading comprehension and information extraction amidst highly redundant and noisy retrieved snippets. • WebShop provides a simulated e-commerce environment grounded in real-world web interactions, featuring over 1.18 million real products and 12,000+ crowdsourced natural language instructions. It requires agents to perform sequential decision-making to search, filter, and purchase target items, systematically evaluating compositional instruction understanding, dynamic query reformulation, and long-horizon multi-step interaction. • FTRL is a foundational evaluation dataset focused on tool-use capabilities, comprising over 2,000 automatically constructed tool interaction scenarios with verifiable execution environments. It typically serves as a basis for in-domain training and evaluation, aiming to systematically measure a model’s tool-calling accuracy and sequential decision-making efficacy within standardized environments. • BFCL (Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard) , proposed by Patil et al., is a comprehensive function-calling evaluation benchmark. Its core dataset encompasses thousands of question-function-answer pairs spanning multiple programming languages and interfaces (e.g., Python, Java, JavaScript, and REST APIs). Through iterative updates, BFCL has expanded to include complex test cases involving multi-turn dialogues, multi-step dependencies, parallel function calls, and real-time dynamic scenarios, primarily assessing a model’s instruction-following capability and dynamic decision-making robustness in real-world API interactions. • ToolHop is a query-driven benchmark specifically designed to evaluate the multi-hop tool use capabilities of large language models. The dataset consists of 995 complex user queries and 3,912 associated locally executable tools. By constructing toolchains with strong interdependencies, it rigorously examines a model’s comprehensive proficiency in long-horizon logical reasoning, dynamic query reformulation, and multi-step tool orchestration.

sections.heading: B.1 Outcome RL and General (Self-) Distillation
sections.text: • GRPO ( Guo et al., 2025 ) is a reinforcement learning method that eliminates the need for an explicit value model. It samples multiple responses for the same input and estimates advantages based on their relative rewards within the group. Its supervision mainly comes from the final task outcome, such that all decisions along a trajectory typically share the same outcome-level reward. • ToolRL ( Qian et al., 2026 ) is a reinforcement learning framework designed for tool-use tasks. It trains tool-using agents with reward signals associated with task outcomes and tool execution, aiming to improve tool selection and invocation capabilities in complex and unseen tool-use scenarios. • MatchTIR ( Qu et al., 2026a ) addresses the coarse-grained credit assignment problem of trajectory-level rewards in multi-turn tool-integrated reasoning. It matches generated tool-use trajectories with reference trajectories via bipartite matching to construct turn-level rewards, and combines trajectory-level and turn-level advantages for more fine-grained policy optimization. • OPD lets the student model generate trajectories under its current policy and queries a teacher model to provide token-level distribution supervision on states visited by the student. Compared with offline distillation, OPD reduces the train–test distribution mismatch by directly training on the student’s on-policy state distribution. • TCOD ( Wang et al., 2026b ) focuses on trajectory-level KL instability caused by error accumulation in multi-turn on-policy distillation. It adopts a temporal curriculum that gradually increases the interaction horizon from short trajectories to full-length trajectories, enabling the student to progressively acquire long-horizon interaction capabilities while improving training stability. • OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) is an on-policy self-distillation approach that removes the dependence on a separate large teacher model. The same model acts as both student and teacher under different contextual conditions: the student generates on-policy trajectories, while a privileged teacher view with additional task information provides token-level supervision. • ATOD Tan et al. (2026b) is a turn-aware on-policy distillation method for long-horizon multi-turn agents. It combines OPD with GRPO through an annealed training scheme and dynamically adjusts the distillation strength at each turn according to teacher–student disagreement and uncertainty, thereby allocating stronger supervision to interaction steps that remain difficult for the student. • TurnSight ( Qu et al., 2026b ) introduces turn-level hindsight self-distillation for tool-integrated reasoning. It constructs a hindsight teacher using tool execution outcomes and measures teacher–student distribution discrepancies at individual turns. Multi-step lookahead and group-wise normalization are further used to assign differentiated supervision weights across tool-interaction turns.

sections.heading: B.2 Skill-Conditioned Self-Distillation
sections.text: • Skill-SD ( Wang et al., 2026a ) is a skill-conditioned self-distillation framework for multi-turn LLM agents. It summarizes completed agent trajectories into compact natural-language skills describing successful behaviors, common mistakes, and reusable workflows, and uses these skills as dynamic privileged information for the teacher branch. The student is then trained to internalize such skill guidance through on-policy distillation, together with an importance-weighted reverse-KL objective and dynamic teacher synchronization for stable training. • SDAR ( Lu et al., 2026 ) integrates on-policy self-distillation into agentic reinforcement learning as a gated auxiliary objective, while retaining RL as the primary optimization signal. It derives token-level teacher–student discrepancy signals and maps them into adaptive gates, strengthening distillation on teacher-endorsed tokens while attenuating unreliable negative guidance, thereby improving training stability in long-horizon multi-turn tasks. • AgentOPSD Wang et al. (2026c) introduces recursive self-distillation for fine-grained credit assignment in long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. It aggregates token-level teacher–student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence and recursively updates a Bayesian belief state across interaction turns, using the resulting belief revisions to estimate the importance of individual decisions and reweight policy optimization without introducing an additional critic or extra rollouts.

sections.heading: Appendix C Implementation Details
sections.text: For the long-horizon tasks reported in Table 1 , we use GRPO as the base policy optimization algorithm and jointly optimize it with the ToolOPD auxiliary objective. ToolOPD operates exclusively on tool-action tokens. For each completed trajectory, the teacher generates an outcome-conditioned hindsight skill, whose effect on the teacher’s action probabilities is converted into fine-grained credit for reweighting the distillation loss. sections.heading: Appendix D Computational Overhead Analysis
sections.text: To quantify the additional computational cost of ToolOPD, we use a matched eight-GPU setup on FTRL and exclude evaluation and checkpointing time from all measurements. As shown in Fig. 7 (d), ToolOPD does not improve raw training throughput: it requires 643 seconds per million training tokens, compared with 151, 177, and 356 seconds for GRPO, MatchTIR, and TurnSight, respectively. The per-rollout cost breakdown in Fig. 7 (c) further shows that ToolOPD is dominated by rollout generation (22.5 GPU-s) and outcome-aware supervision construction (8.8 GPU-s), whereas policy updates account for only a small fraction of the total cost (2.1 GPU-s). These results indicate that the additional overhead primarily arises from teacher-driven hindsight skill inference and action-level supervision construction, rather than standard policy optimization. Despite this overhead, the performance–cost curve in Fig. 7 (b) reveals a favorable optimization trade-off in some regimes. In particular, Fig. 7 (a) shows that ToolOPD reaches an F1 score of 21% after 18.2 GPU-hours, requiring less computation than GRPO (19.5 GPU-hours) and substantially less than TurnSight (57.0 GPU-hours), although it remains more expensive than MatchTIR (12.5 GPU-hours). Therefore, ToolOPD should not be viewed as a method for improving raw computational efficiency; instead, it trades additional computation for more targeted credit assignment, allowing it to reach a comparable performance level with lower cost than TurnSight.

Affiliation: Northeastern University Zhengzong Chen Yuanyuan Zhao Affiliation: Honor Device Co., Ltd Fei Huang Affiliation: Honor Device Co., Ltd Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) enhances the capabilities of small language agents by providing dense, token-level supervision from a teacher model on student-generated trajectories. However, standard OPD implicitly assumes that credit is uniformly distributed across long-horizon trajectories, assigning the same strength of teacher supervision to different actions. Through credit-distribution analysis and outcome-reversal counterfactual experiments, we find that trajectory credit is concentrated on a small number of critical actions. Moreover, even when the trajectory is held fixed, reversing only the final outcome substantially changes the credit assigned to multiple interaction turns. These findings show that the uniform-credit assumption fails to identify critical decisions and ultimately degrades the model’s reasoning accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose ToolOPD , an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework designed for long-horizon tool use. ToolOPD first summarizes each completed trajectory and its outcome into a reusable hindsight skill. It then measures how this skill changes the teacher’s probability of each student action token and converts the change into outcome-aware credit. The resulting credit preserves supervision that supports successful decisions or discourages failed ones, while suppressing irrelevant and conflicting signals. ToolOPD uses these credits to reweight the action-level distillation loss and jointly optimizes it with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across multiple long-horizon tool interaction benchmarks demonstrate that ToolOPD significantly outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines. https://github.com/MagicAgent-Search/ToolOPD 1 Introduction Figure 1: Empirical Study Results. Large language models (LLMs) ( Naveed et al., 2025 ; Minaee et al., 2024 ; Chang et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2026b ; Thirunavukarasu et al., 2023 ) have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex interactive tasks by invoking external tools ( Qu et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Qin et al., 2024 ) and adapting their decisions to environmental feedback. However, long-horizon tool-use tasks ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) often require tens or hundreds of interaction turns while providing only a sparse success-or-failure reward at the end of the trajectory. This makes it difficult to determine which intermediate actions contribute to the final outcome. On-policy distillation (OPD) ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Song and Zheng, 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) addresses sparse supervision by matching a compact student policy to a teacher distribution on trajectories generated by the student itself. Standard OPD implicitly assumes that credit is uniformly distributed across long-horizon trajectories, such that different actions receive equal credit and the same strength of teacher supervision. This uniform credit assignment fails to distinguish critical tool decisions from routine transitional actions, thereby weakening effective supervision for critical decisions. To systematically characterize this issue, we conduct a series of empirical studies. As shown in Fig. 1 (a), on the ALFWorld diagnostic trajectories, the top 20% of interaction turns account for 74.2% of the total credit, demonstrating that trajectory credit is highly concentrated rather than uniformly distributed. We further construct an outcome-reversal counterfactual experiment by fixing the complete task and state–action sequence while reversing only the outcome label provided to the teacher. Fig. 1 (b) shows that this intervention substantially changes the credit assigned to 55.2%, 25.0%, and 50.0% of interaction turns in ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA, respectively. Thus, the credit of an action depends not only on its local context but also on its relationship with the final outcome. Fig. 1 (c) further shows that outcome-conflicting signals account for 53.5% of the total teacher evidence under uniform distillation. Together, these findings establish that effective long-horizon distillation must identify critical actions and determine whether the corresponding teacher signals are consistent with the trajectory outcome. Detailed settings are provided in Appendix H . Recent studies have begun to explore fine-grained credit assignment for long-horizon tasks. ATOD ( Tan et al., 2026b ) adaptively adjusts the distillation strength of different actions according to the discrepancy between the teacher and student policies, while TurnSight ( Qu et al., 2026b ) constructs multi-view hindsight information from actual tool executions and selects reliable turn-level supervision through cross-view consistency. Unlike existing methods that determine distillation weights from local teacher–student divergence, training progress, or interaction difficulty, in this work, we propose ToolOPD , an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework for long-horizon tool use. ToolOPD uses the terminal outcome to determine both the direction and strength of action credit. For each student-generated trajectory, ToolOPD conditions the teacher on the complete interaction process and its outcome to induce a concise hindsight skill that summarizes the effective workflow or failure pattern. It then compares the teacher’s action probabilities with and without the hindsight skill to estimate the outcome-relevant credit of each action token. For successful trajectories, ToolOPD retains skill-induced probability increases that reinforce effective actions; for failed trajectories, it retains probability decreases that suppress erroneous actions. The resulting relevance is further calibrated by teacher confidence and experience-based reliability to prevent uncertain or historically inconsistent teacher signals from dominating the update. ToolOPD uses the calibrated credit to dynamically reweight the distillation loss over <action> tokens and jointly optimizes it with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . This design concentrates supervision on outcome-relevant decisions while filtering redundant and conflicting signals. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • Empirical findings. We show that credit in long-horizon OPD is concentrated on critical actions and depends on trajectory outcomes, while uniform distillation transfers outcome-conflicting supervision. • Method. We propose ToolOPD, which induces outcome-conditioned hindsight skills and converts their effects on teacher predictions into fine-grained, outcome-asymmetric action credit. • Experiments. Across multiple tool-use benchmarks and model scales, ToolOPD consistently outperforms representative reinforcement learning and OPD baselines in task performance, long-context robustness, and optimization stability. 2 Method 2.1 Problem Formulation We consider multi-turn tool use tasks with a discrete set of executable actions. In long-horizon tool use scenarios, this setting introduces severe credit assignment challenges: due to the extremely long interaction horizon and highly sparse rewards, the success or failure of a task is typically determined by only a few critical tool decisions (e.g., specific API selections or parameter settings), while the vast majority of the remaining turns consist of routine state queries and transitional actions. How to accurately attribute and assign the terminal global reward to the intermediate specific actions is the core difficulty in optimizing such policies. We are given a teacher model π ϕ \pi_{\phi} with frozen parameters. Our objective is to distill the transferable strategy summarized by the teacher based on the complete trajectory and the final outcome into the student, while preserving the exploration capability of on-policy reinforcement learning. Therefore, our method falls under the category of On-Policy Distillation, rather than simple behavior cloning on offline teacher trajectories. 2.2 Overview of ToolOPD To address the credit assignment dilemma caused by sparse rewards in long-horizon interactions, ToolOPD organically integrates GRPO with outcome-aware on-policy distillation. Its core idea is to transform sparse trajectory-level credit into dense action-level credit. The specific data flow is as follows: First, the student policy interacts with the environment to generate a set of on-policy trajectories, and the intra-group relative advantages for GRPO are computed. Subsequently, the teacher reads the complete trajectory and the final success/failure outcome to induce a concise, reusable hindsight skill. Next, by comparing the probability distributions of the teacher with and without this skill on the student’s actions, the outcome relevance of the skill to the current action is calculated, thereby achieving fine-grained credit assignment. Finally, a weighted teacher-to-student OPD is performed exclusively on the action ( <action> ) tokens. Throughout the training process, the teacher model parameters remain frozen, and all gradients are used solely to update the student model. The framework of ToolOPD is illustrated in Fig. 2 . As shown in Fig. 6 (a), ToolOPD achieves an average success rate of 59.38%, outperforming Vanilla OPD and Skill-OPD by 5.47 and 4.69 percentage points, respectively. As the retained proportion increases, the differences gradually diminish and eventually converge. These results demonstrate that ToolOPD effectively ranks turns according to supervision quality and prioritizes distillation signals associated with tool decisions that are more likely to affect the final outcome. Taken together, Fig. 6 (a) and (b) suggest that the performance gains of ToolOPD primarily arise from fine-grained, outcome-aware credit assignment, rather than merely introducing additional teacher supervision. 4 Related Work 4.1 On-policy Distillation On-policy distillation (OPD) ( Song and Zheng, 2026 ) aligns the student and teacher policies by matching the student policy to the teacher distribution over its self-generated trajectories. By utilizing objectives such as token-level KL divergence, OPD effectively mitigates the state distribution shift inherent in offline distillation. As OPD is extended to long-horizon agent tasks, research has transitioned from uniform token-level matching to step- or turn-level supervision. In Toolintegrated scenarios, existing approaches primarily operate along two dimensions. First, they leverage dynamic skills or hindsight information from completed trajectories to guide self-distillation (including Skill-SD ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , SEED ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , and TurnSight Qu et al. (2026b) ). Second, they dynamically adjust the distillation weights across interaction turns based on factors including teacher-student divergence, training budgets, and interaction difficulty (including SOD ( Zhong et al., 2026 ) , TurnOPD ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , AgentOPSD ( Wang et al., 2026c ) , and HIDIFFTIR ( Guo et al., 2026 ) ). These studies demonstrate that online distillation for Toolusing agents must model multi-turn interaction structures, tool invocation difficulty, and hindsight information, rather than relying on uniform token-level supervision. In contrast to existing methods, this paper focuses on the credit assignment problem for small models executing tool invocations in long-horizon tasks on resource-constrained terminal devices. We propose ToolOPD, which moves beyond the reliance on local training difficulty or teacher-student divergence by directly evaluating the true contribution of tool decisions based on final task outcomes. The core of ToolOPD lies in performing non-uniform credit assignment for distinct tool decisions and dynamically adjusting the distillation intensity of action tokens accordingly, thereby maximizing the distillation efficacy of small models under resource constraints. 4.2 Credit Assignment in Long-Horizon On-Policy Distillation In long-horizon tool use tasks ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2026 ) , standard OPD typically performs uniform token-level distribution matching across all visited states. However, because different interaction turns contribute unequally to task success, applying supervision with uniform intensity is highly prone to introducing noise. Recent studies have introduced fine-grained credit assignment into long-horizon interactions and policy distillation. Some methods evaluate intermediate action values by quantifying information gain, leveraging hindsight information, or decomposing trajectory-level outcomes (e.g., Δ \Delta Belief-RL ( Auzina et al., 2026 ) , HCAPO ( Tan et al., 2026a ) , and PBSD ( Tian et al., 2026 ) ). Others identify critical action spans and adjust local advantages from the perspectives of supervision reliability, failure correlation, or policy comparison (e.g., Prune-OPD ( Yang et al., 2026b ) , HINT-SD ( Yeo et al., 2026 ) , UCOB ( Tu et al., 2026 ) , and SGCD ( Ding et al., 2026 ) ). Overall, existing research has transitioned from uniform token-level matching to credit-aware selective supervision. In this work, ToolOPD locates critical tool decisions by quantifying the shift in the teacher’s action distribution conditioned on hindsight skills. It then performs multi-dimensional credit calibration by integrating the final outcome, trajectory consistency, and teacher confidence. Ultimately, the calibrated turn-level credit is directly mapped to the action tokens actually sampled by the student, achieving non-uniform on-policy distillation oriented towards long-horizon task outcomes. 5 Conclusion We introduce ToolOPD, an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework that addresses credit assignment in long-horizon tool-use tasks. Our empirical analysis shows that the uniform supervision of standard OPD fails to distinguish the contributions of different tool decisions and may introduce teacher signals that conflict with the final outcome. To address this limitation, ToolOPD induces hindsight skills from complete trajectories and their outcomes, and dynamically assigns credit to action tokens through outcome-asymmetric skill relevance. This preserves supervision consistent with the task outcome while suppressing irrelevant or conflicting signals. Experiments across multiple long-horizon tool-interaction benchmarks and model scales demonstrate that ToolOPD consistently outperforms reinforcement-learning and on-policy-distillation baselines while exhibiting more stable optimization over extended interactions. Appendix Contents Appendix A Benchmarks • ALFWorld is an interactive benchmark that aligns abstract textual reasoning with concrete embodied environments, requiring agents to translate high-level text policies into multi-step navigation and object manipulation actions in simulated household settings, thereby evaluating cross-modal grounding and long-horizon planning. • SearchQA is a large-scale open-domain question answering dataset comprising over 140,000 question-answer pairs augmented with real-world search engine contexts, designed to assess model robustness in precise machine reading comprehension and information extraction amidst highly redundant and noisy retrieved snippets. • WebShop provides a simulated e-commerce environment grounded in real-world web interactions, featuring over 1.18 million real products and 12,000+ crowdsourced natural language instructions. It requires agents to perform sequential decision-making to search, filter, and purchase target items, systematically evaluating compositional instruction understanding, dynamic query reformulation, and long-horizon multi-step interaction. • FTRL is a foundational evaluation dataset focused on tool-use capabilities, comprising over 2,000 automatically constructed tool interaction scenarios with verifiable execution environments. It typically serves as a basis for in-domain training and evaluation, aiming to systematically measure a model’s tool-calling accuracy and sequential decision-making efficacy within standardized environments. • BFCL (Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard) , proposed by Patil et al., is a comprehensive function-calling evaluation benchmark. Its core dataset encompasses thousands of question-function-answer pairs spanning multiple programming languages and interfaces (e.g., Python, Java, JavaScript, and REST APIs). Through iterative updates, BFCL has expanded to include complex test cases involving multi-turn dialogues, multi-step dependencies, parallel function calls, and real-time dynamic scenarios, primarily assessing a model’s instruction-following capability and dynamic decision-making robustness in real-world API interactions. • ToolHop is a query-driven benchmark specifically designed to evaluate the multi-hop tool use capabilities of large language models. The dataset consists of 995 complex user queries and 3,912 associated locally executable tools. By constructing toolchains with strong interdependencies, it rigorously examines a model’s comprehensive proficiency in long-horizon logical reasoning, dynamic query reformulation, and multi-step tool orchestration. Appendix B Baselines B.1 Outcome RL and General (Self-) Distillation • GRPO ( Guo et al., 2025 ) is a reinforcement learning method that eliminates the need for an explicit value model. It samples multiple responses for the same input and estimates advantages based on their relative rewards within the group. Its supervision mainly comes from the final task outcome, such that all decisions along a trajectory typically share the same outcome-level reward. • ToolRL ( Qian et al., 2026 ) is a reinforcement learning framework designed for tool-use tasks. It trains tool-using agents with reward signals associated with task outcomes and tool execution, aiming to improve tool selection and invocation capabilities in complex and unseen tool-use scenarios. • MatchTIR ( Qu et al., 2026a ) addresses the coarse-grained credit assignment problem of trajectory-level rewards in multi-turn tool-integrated reasoning. It matches generated tool-use trajectories with reference trajectories via bipartite matching to construct turn-level rewards, and combines trajectory-level and turn-level advantages for more fine-grained policy optimization. • OPD lets the student model generate trajectories under its current policy and queries a teacher model to provide token-level distribution supervision on states visited by the student. Compared with offline distillation, OPD reduces the train–test distribution mismatch by directly training on the student’s on-policy state distribution. • TCOD ( Wang et al., 2026b ) focuses on trajectory-level KL instability caused by error accumulation in multi-turn on-policy distillation. It adopts a temporal curriculum that gradually increases the interaction horizon from short trajectories to full-length trajectories, enabling the student to progressively acquire long-horizon interaction capabilities while improving training stability. • OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) is an on-policy self-distillation approach that removes the dependence on a separate large teacher model. The same model acts as both student and teacher under different contextual conditions: the student generates on-policy trajectories, while a privileged teacher view with additional task information provides token-level supervision. • ATOD Tan et al. (2026b) is a turn-aware on-policy distillation method for long-horizon multi-turn agents. It combines OPD with GRPO through an annealed training scheme and dynamically adjusts the distillation strength at each turn according to teacher–student disagreement and uncertainty, thereby allocating stronger supervision to interaction steps that remain difficult for the student. • TurnSight ( Qu et al., 2026b ) introduces turn-level hindsight self-distillation for tool-integrated reasoning. It constructs a hindsight teacher using tool execution outcomes and measures teacher–student distribution discrepancies at individual turns. Multi-step lookahead and group-wise normalization are further used to assign differentiated supervision weights across tool-interaction turns. B.2 Skill-Conditioned Self-Distillation • Skill-SD ( Wang et al., 2026a ) is a skill-conditioned self-distillation framework for multi-turn LLM agents. It summarizes completed agent trajectories into compact natural-language skills describing successful behaviors, common mistakes, and reusable workflows, and uses these skills as dynamic privileged information for the teacher branch. The student is then trained to internalize such skill guidance through on-policy distillation, together with an importance-weighted reverse-KL objective and dynamic teacher synchronization for stable training. • SDAR ( Lu et al., 2026 ) integrates on-policy self-distillation into agentic reinforcement learning as a gated auxiliary objective, while retaining RL as the primary optimization signal. It derives token-level teacher–student discrepancy signals and maps them into adaptive gates, strengthening distillation on teacher-endorsed tokens while attenuating unreliable negative guidance, thereby improving training stability in long-horizon multi-turn tasks. • AgentOPSD Wang et al. (2026c) introduces recursive self-distillation for fine-grained credit assignment in long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. It aggregates token-level teacher–student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence and recursively updates a Bayesian belief state across interaction turns, using the resulting belief revisions to estimate the importance of individual decisions and reweight policy optimization without introducing an additional critic or extra rollouts. Appendix D Computational Overhead Analysis To quantify the additional computational cost of ToolOPD, we use a matched eight-GPU setup on FTRL and exclude evaluation and checkpointing time from all measurements. As shown in Fig. 7 (d), ToolOPD does not improve raw training throughput: it requires 643 seconds per million training tokens, compared with 151, 177, and 356 seconds for GRPO, MatchTIR, and TurnSight, respectively. The per-rollout cost breakdown in Fig. 7 (c) further shows that ToolOPD is dominated by rollout generation (22.5 GPU-s) and outcome-aware supervision construction (8.8 GPU-s), whereas policy updates account for only a small fraction of the total cost (2.1 GPU-s). These results indicate that the additional overhead primarily arises from teacher-driven hindsight skill inference and action-level supervision construction, rather than standard policy optimization. Despite this overhead, the performance–cost curve in Fig. 7 (b) reveals a favorable optimization trade-off in some regimes. In particular, Fig. 7 (a) shows that ToolOPD reaches an F1 score of 21% after 18.2 GPU-hours, requiring less computation than GRPO (19.5 GPU-hours) and substantially less than TurnSight (57.0 GPU-hours), although it remains more expensive than MatchTIR (12.5 GPU-hours). Therefore, ToolOPD should not be viewed as a method for improving raw computational efficiency; instead, it trades additional computation for more targeted credit assignment, allowing it to reach a comparable performance level with lower cost than TurnSight.
